## TL;DR

A server restart can leave an in-flight engineer harness alive as an orphan, and RepoOS re-attaches it ("adopted orphaned engineer pid N"). The reported symptom was that adopted engineers then went idle, queued messages were never delivered, and the board only ever said "an undelivered message is already queued".

The task's stated hypothesis — that the adopted process lost its stdout/stdin link to the new server — is wrong, and I recorded why so it is not "fixed" again. Engineers are spawned with stdout and stderr on file descriptors, not server-owned pipes, precisely so a reload cannot cause EPIPE; stdin is always ignored. After adoption the server replays `<taskId>.out.log` and tails it from the end, so output, handoff signals and `repoos mv` request files keep working.

What actually breaks is turn-end classification. An adopted entry has no `ChildProcess` handle, so the `close` event that carries an exit code never fires in the new server; `reconcileDeadAgents()` is the only observer, and it passed `exitedCleanly: false` for every adopted turn. Each adopted turn that ended normally was booked as a crash, escalated to `needs_input`, and had its queued messages handed to crash recovery instead of being delivered. A second gap made the wait unbounded: while an adopted process is alive but silent, the CTO nudge holds on `message-queued` and `restart-stalled-agent` refuses because `isRunning()` is true.

## Work and rationale

Two fixes, deliberately separate because they cover different shapes.

First, an adopted turn's end is now clean unless there is positive evidence otherwise: a replayed provider failure, a missing worktree, or an abort RepoOS itself issued. With no exit code there is no evidence of failure, so treating an unknown adopted exit as a crash was the wrong default. A clean classification routes the turn through the existing bounded clean-exit resume policy and lets the normal end-of-turn path deliver any queued message.

Second, I added a bounded recovery for a run that is alive but not progressing. `recoverSilentEngineerWithQueuedMessage()` ends the turn when the oldest queued message has waited past an hour and the engineer has produced no output. Ending the turn is what delivers the queue, so the engineer resumes with the message. The decision is a pure function in `src/core/queued-message-recovery.ts` with conservative guards: no known long-running work child (check, tests, build, browser, remote validation), not paused, not handing off, process group still alive (a dead group belongs to phantom-runner recovery), and not already recovering.

The watchdog offers each active task with a queue to the runner each tick. Paused, held, archived, needs-input and human-assigned tasks are skipped at the watchdog, and the runner re-checks the same gates. I also added SIGKILL escalation for adopted turns, because an adopted process has no `close` event to force the issue if it ignores SIGTERM.

The finding and both mechanisms are documented in `docs/agent-run-operations.md`, with a cross-reference from `docs/cto-autopilot.md` so the "undelivered message queued" hold is not read as indefinite.

## Approaches tried

I started from the task's hypothesis and tested it against the code and the 2026-11-03 activity logs. The spawn path clearly gives the child file descriptors rather than pipes, with a comment explaining that this is exactly to survive a reload, and stdin is `"ignore"` for every engineer. The logs also show continued worktree edits after each adoption line, which rules out a dead output channel.

I then traced what is genuinely different about an adopted entry: no `proc`, therefore no exit event, therefore finalisation depends on the watchdog's liveness sweep. Reading that sweep showed the hardcoded `exitedCleanly: false`, which explained the repeated "agent exited with an error" and `needs_input` lines in the incident tasks.

For the queue I considered reusing the CTO nudge, but a nudge is just another queued message, so it cannot unblock anything. Treating an overdue queued message as a restart candidate also fails, because that path refuses while a turn is running. Ending the turn and letting the existing delivery path run is the smallest change that actually delivers.

I rejected a broader "restart any silent engineer" rule: a long check or a slow model call is not a stall, and the process-group inspection already distinguishes known work children.

## Challenges and blockers

The incident evidence is noisy because the machine was heavily loaded: the logs show load around 8.5x per CPU, repeated check-slot waits and "slot holder has made no progress" escalations. Some reported "idle" windows were genuinely slow work rather than a lost channel, so I kept the new recovery conservative and gated on a full hour plus current silence.

A live reproduction would require restarting the control-plane server mid-turn, which is server-owned and not something an engineer session should do. I reproduced the mechanism from the adoption and finalisation code plus the recorded activity, and covered the behaviour with tests instead.

One pre-existing test failure (`does not escalate a wait under ten minutes`) reproduces identically on `main`; it depends on the host's real local-check slot state rather than this change.

## Key learnings

An "unknown exit" is not a "failed exit". Defaulting to failure looked safe but silently changed lifecycle behaviour: it parked tasks on a human and rerouted queued messages into crash recovery. When a process is adopted rather than spawned, the absence of an exit code is the normal case, not an error signal.

Recovery policies that hold on one signal need a bound somewhere else. The idle nudge correctly refused to add noise behind a queued message, and the restart action correctly refused to act on a "running" turn; together they left no path forward. The fix belongs where the turn can actually be ended, not in either policy alone.
